source.title: A Unified Mechanistic Analysis of Knowledge- and Safety-Based Refusals
source.authors: Yu-Sin Son; Seunghee Kim; Hyuhng Joon Kim; Taeuk Kim

page_placements.theme: Refusal direction vs directions for other non-answering behaviours (abstention, hedging, incapability, bail, derailing, privacy refusal): overlap and specificity

record.tranche_reason: The study measures difference-in-means refusal directions and steers them, and refines a single-direction account with evidence for a dominant shared component plus persistent type-specific residuals and asymmetric transfer.
record.gate_note: The study estimates matched KR–KC and SR–SC activation shifts and reports their alignment, cross-type probe transfer, and behavioral activation-steering effects. It does not project a direction out of every layer and position or report refusal behavior after such removal. Values shown only in figures are recorded as figure-only. Other training-checkpoint benchmark results are not rows because they do not measure the estimated directions’ effects.
record.test_reason: The study estimates difference-in-means refusal directions (SR−SC, plus a knowledge-refusal KR−KC analogue) and adds them to the residual stream to induce refusal (V1, addition only). It decomposes them into a dominant common component plus type-specific residuals (V4). There is no ablation, weight edit, jailbreak, reasoning-model or cross-language test.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that knowledge- and safety-based refusals share a dominant refusal direction, with asymmetric overlap (SR→KR stronger than KR→SR). Type-specific epistemic vs normative features emerge sharply in the final layers. They describe refusal as 'commit-then-specify'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means shifts between matched refusal and control prompts and activation steering, but estimates separate KR and SR directions, extracts activations at the final prompt-token position, and steers at a selected peak-alignment layer rather than testing a single harmful-minus-harmless direction with ablation across all layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effect varies by model family and intervention strength; the paper reports stronger effects for Llama∗ and Qwen∗ and weaker positive effects for Gemma∗. Direction alignment and transfer also vary across models and layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-refusal probes transfer to knowledge refusal (0.80–0.86) far better than the reverse (0.58–0.63). The gap holds in base and tuned models, under both tuning orders, and in two newer models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal directions for different refusal grounds overlap asymmetrically: the safety-refusal direction captures more of a shared refusal component than the knowledge-refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a knowledge-refusal (fictional-minus-answerable) direction also induces refusal: large in Llama∗, moderate in Qwen∗, weak in Gemma∗. Type-specific residual steering shifts the rationale toward epistemic or normative framing (Fig. 9, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-safety refusal (abstention for lack of knowledge) is also mediated by a steerable direction largely shared with safety refusal.

record.problems: Behavioral steering results are shown in a figure without numeric values in the text. The steering test adds directions only at a selected layer and does not test removal or capability costs. The paper notes its matched benchmark is a controlled diagnostic set and focuses on single-turn prompts.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted tuning-checkpoint benchmark results in Table 4 because they evaluate tuned behavior and general performance, not the estimated direction intervention. Omitted attention-head and MLP ablations because their reported outcome is change in diagnostic projection, not refusal behavior; the authors also state these do not establish a complete causal circuit.

untested.parts: Ablation of the direction (removing refusal) and retention of other abilities after intervention. Only addition at one peak layer is tested.
Affine or cone formulations, and multi-dimensionality within harmful refusal alone. The 'other' component here separates knowledge from safety refusal.
Harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision is not separated.
No cross-language or cross-model direction transfer. Base vs tuned models are compared only in alignment and probe statistics, not by transferring a direction.
Tuning order is varied, but only probe transfer is reported, not whether a removable direction exists.

missing.what: Cross-type probe transfer for the two additional recent models (Qwen3.5-9B 0.836/0.580; Gemma-3-12B 0.841/0.608)
XSTest-derived set (N=125) replication for Qwen3.5-9B: peak shift alignment 0.756 vs 0.781; probe transfer 0.824/0.592
Random unit-vector steering control said to confirm direction specificity; no numbers given
Numeric refusal-rate changes per model, direction and α for steering (only in figure)

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The V1-relevant direction is only SR−SC (sensitive vs benign-matched prompts), close to but narrower than harmful-minus-harmless. Hidden states come from the final prompt token, and steering is applied at a single selected layer. The refusal classifier is lexical. KR-direction results are kept out of V1 because V1 names a harm-based direction. V4 support concerns multiplicity across refusal grounds, not within safety refusal.

versions.untested_parts: Tests adding estimated KR and SR directions at a selected peak-alignment layer, not ablating a single direction from every layer and position; does not test whether general capability is retained after direction ablation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No attack is tested as suppressing a refusal direction, and no training against such ablation is evaluated.
Tests a dominant common direction and type-specific residuals; does not test affine or cone formulations specifically, nor establish a complete causal circuit for refusal.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.

Does not test whether the same estimated direction transfers across languages or whether a direction from one model variant transfers to another; KR-to-SR and SR-to-KR probe transfer are different tests.
Compares training orders for cross-type probe transfer, but does not test whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
